card.thesis: In heavily-optioned, high-open-interest instruments (broad index ETFs and major sector SPDRs), a period of contracting realized volatility is systematically accompanied by net-short-gamma positioning among option sellers -- covered-call overlay funds, options-income strategies, and dealer desks that have sold volatility into the calm and hedge by trading against price. While the range holds, that flow is stabilizing: dealers buy dips and sell rips, compressing range further. When price finally closes outside the upper band while realized volatility (ATR-14) is still below its own longer-run baseline (ATR-50), the move has started before the option-selling crowd has repriced -- their short-gamma hedging flips from stabilizing to reinforcing (short calls forces the dealer/writer to buy into the breakout to stay hedged), mechanically extending the initial move for a period afterward. The other side of this trade is the option seller who wrote premium assuming continued range-bound behavior and is now a forced, mechanical buyer. What is expected to go wrong: this mechanism is about the first burst of a volatility regime change, not persistence. In a slow grinding bear (rate-driven, low realized-vol decline) there may be few or no valid low-ATR breakouts to trade, and the strategy should sit mostly in cash -- underperforming a benchmark that keeps drifting down slowly without ever tripping the squeeze condition. It is also vulnerable to a crash that gaps straight through the band with ATR already elevated (already-expanded, not compressed, volatility) -- COVID's opening days looked like that -- in which case the squeeze filter correctly refuses the entry, but a separate, unfiltered breakout would have caught the early down-move it is not designed to catch (this strategy is long-only).
card.entry: close crosses_above bb_upper(20,2.0) and atr(14) < atr(50)
